title: THE SEA HAD JUST SWALLOWED THEIR ENEMIES… THEN MIRIAM PICKED UP A TAMBOURINE
paragraphs: THE SEA HAD JUST SWALLOWED THEIR ENEMIES… THEN MIRIAM PICKED UP A TAMBOURINE
Before Israel could build a home in freedom, a woman stepped out of the shadow of slavery and taught a generation how to worship the God who had brought them through the impossible.
“And Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a timbrel in her hand; and all the women went out after her with timbrels and with dances.” — Exodus 15:20 (KJV)
Imagine standing on the other side of a sea that should have been your grave.
Your feet are trembling.
Your clothes still carry the dust of a land where your people were treated like property.
Behind you lies the water.
And somewhere beneath those waves is the army that had been determined to drag you back into slavery.
You can still remember the sound of the chariots.
The screaming.
The terror.
The terrible moment when you looked ahead and saw nothing but water, looked behind and saw Pharaoh's soldiers, and realized there was nowhere left to run.
And then…
God made a way.
Not around the sea.
Not over the sea.
Through it.
Now imagine a woman reaching for a tambourine.
Not because she has forgotten the suffering.
Not because every wound has healed.
Not because she knows what tomorrow will bring.
But because she knows who brought them through yesterday.
Her name was Miriam.
And what happened when she lifted that tambourine was more than a celebration.
It was a declaration that the God who had heard the cries of slaves had not abandoned His people.
But there is something even more extraordinary hidden in this story.
Something about Miriam's past.
Something about her future.

And something about the Gospel of Jesus Christ that turns this ancient moment of worship into a mirror for every wounded soul that has ever wondered whether God could still write a beautiful ending from a painful beginning.
Because Miriam's story does not begin with music.
It begins under the shadow of death.
Long before she stood beside the sea, Miriam belonged to a people living under oppression in Egypt.
Pharaoh had ordered that Hebrew baby boys be thrown into the Nile (Exodus 1:22).
Think about that.
A river that should have sustained life had become an instrument of terror.
Mothers feared for their children.
Families lived beneath the cruelty of a ruler who believed he could control the future by destroying the vulnerable.
And in Exodus 2, a young girl stood at a distance, watching a basket hidden among the reeds.
Inside was her baby brother.
Moses.
The child who would one day stand before Pharaoh.
The child whom God would use to lead Israel out of Egypt.
But at that moment, he was simply a helpless baby floating on a dangerous river.
And his sister was watching.
Exodus 2:4 says:
“And his sister stood afar off, to wit what would be done to him.” (KJV)
The passage does not name her there, but the wider biblical account identifies Miriam as the sister of Moses and Aaron.
She was there before the burning bush.
Before the plagues.
Before the sea opened.
Before anyone in Israel sang about victory.
She was there when the future looked like a basket that could disappear beneath the water.
And when Pharaoh's daughter discovered the child, that young sister stepped forward with a question that helped reunite Moses with his own mother as his nurse.
It was a small act in the eyes of the world.
But small acts of courage can become part of a story much larger than the person who performs them.
Perhaps that is where this story first finds you.
Because some of you have been watching over things you cannot control.
A child who has wandered from God.
A marriage that feels fragile.
A parent whose health is failing.
A family drowning in debt.
A prayer you have whispered so many times that you no longer know what words to use.
You have done what you could.
You have stood at a distance.
You have watched.
You have prayed.
And you have wondered whether God was watching too.
Miriam's early story reminds us that God's providence can be at work even when His full purpose is hidden from our eyes.
But Scripture does not promise that every endangered child will be rescued in the same way Moses was, or that every earthly crisis will end the way we desire.
What it reveals is a God who sees affliction, hears the cries of His people, and remains faithful to His covenant.
And generations later, that same Miriam would stand beside another body of water.
Only this time, the waters would not threaten her baby brother.
They would become the setting of God's deliverance of an entire nation.
When Israel reached the Red Sea, the people were trapped between Pharaoh's army and the water.
Exodus 14:10 tells us that they were terribly afraid.
They cried out.
They questioned Moses.
They even suggested that slavery might have been preferable to dying in the wilderness.
Fear can do that to people.
It can make the chains of yesterday appear safer than the uncertainty of tomorrow.
It can make bondage feel familiar enough to mistake for security.
Some of us understand that more than we want to admit.
We know what it means to return mentally to places God has called us to leave.
To revisit destructive relationships.
To excuse hidden sin.
To cling to bitterness because forgiveness feels too vulnerable.
To hold on to an identity built around our worst mistakes because we cannot imagine who we would be without them.
But listen to what Moses told the terrified Israelites.
“Fear ye not, stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD.” — Exodus 14:13 (KJV)
The Hebrew word translated “salvation” is יְשׁוּעָה — yeshu'ah, meaning salvation, deliverance, or rescue.
This is not a secret code inserted into the passage.
It is an ordinary and powerful Hebrew word describing the deliverance God was about to accomplish.
And that distinction matters.
Because the Bible is already extraordinary without forcing hidden meanings into its words.
The name Jesus, through its Hebrew and Aramaic background, is related to the Hebrew name Yeshua, associated with the truth that the LORD saves.
But Exodus 14 is first telling us about God's historical rescue of Israel from Egypt.
We honor the Scripture when we allow that original meaning to stand.
And from the vantage point of the New Testament, we can see how the Exodus becomes part of the larger biblical story of redemption fulfilled in Jesus Christ.
At the sea, God delivered His people from Pharaoh's power.
At the cross and through His resurrection, Jesus accomplished the greater deliverance that sinners desperately need: rescue from sin, condemnation, and death.
The connection is beautiful precisely because it does not require us to distort either story.
Now return to that shoreline.
Moses stretched out his hand as the LORD commanded.
God drove back the sea.
The waters divided.
Israel crossed on dry ground.
And when the Egyptians pursued them, the waters returned.
Exodus 14:30 records:
“Thus the LORD saved Israel that day out of the hand of the Egyptians.” (KJV)
Notice who received the credit.
Not Moses.
Not Miriam.
Not the strength of the Israelites.
The LORD.
Their deliverance was not a monument to human determination.
It was a testimony to divine power and covenant faithfulness.
And this is where the music begins.
Exodus 15 opens with Moses and the Israelites singing to the LORD.
Their song declares:
“The LORD is my strength and song, and he is become my salvation.” — Exodus 15:2 (KJV)
Then, in verses 20 and 21, Miriam steps into the scene.
The Hebrew text says:
וַתִּקַּח מִרְיָם הַנְּבִיאָה אֲחוֹת אַהֲרֹן אֶת־הַתֹּף בְּיָדָהּ
Vattiqqaḥ Miryam hannevi'ah, aḥot Aharon, et-hattof beyadah.
A faithful translation is:
“And Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took the tambourine in her hand.”
The Hebrew calls Miriam הַנְּבִיאָה — hannevi'ah, “the prophetess.”
This is not a title we need to invent to make her important.
Scripture itself gives it to her.
The instrument, תֹּף — tof, was a hand percussion instrument commonly translated as a tambourine or timbrel.
The text then says the women went out after her with tambourines and dancing.
This was not a private emotional reaction.
It was a public celebration of what the LORD had done.
And Miriam called them to sing:
שִׁירוּ לַיהוָה כִּי־גָאֹה גָּאָה סוּס וְרֹכְבוֹ רָמָה בַיָּם
Shiru la-YHWH ki-ga'oh ga'ah; sus verokhevo ramah vayyam.
“Sing ye to the LORD, for he hath triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider hath he thrown into the sea.” — Exodus 15:21 (KJV)
The opening word, שִׁירוּ — shiru, is a plural imperative.
“Sing!”
It is a summons to others.
Miriam was not simply keeping a moment of gratitude to herself.
She was inviting the women to join in declaring the LORD's victory.
And there is something profoundly moving about that.
The woman who once watched over her brother beside the Nile now led other women in worship beside the sea.
The same God who had preserved Moses through the waters of his infancy had used Moses to lead Israel through the waters of deliverance.
Scripture does not tell us what Miriam was thinking in that moment.
We should not pretend to know the private thoughts God has not revealed.
But the contrast between those two scenes is impossible to ignore.
Once, she watched a basket on the water.
Now, she watched a nation standing safely beyond it.
Once, Pharaoh had used the Nile as a weapon against Hebrew children.
Now, Pharaoh's military power had been defeated in the sea.
And the response was worship.
Not worship of Miriam.
Not worship of Moses.
Worship of the LORD.
That is the heart of this passage.
The tambourine was in Miriam's hand, but the glory belonged to God.
And perhaps that is exactly what someone reading this needs to remember.
Because we live in a world that teaches us to celebrate ourselves.
Our success.
Our resilience.
Our achievements.
Our ability to overcome.
And there is a place for gratitude over the courage and perseverance God enables.
But Miriam's song points beyond the instrument, beyond the leader, and beyond the people.
It points to the One who saved them.
What if the greatest testimony of your life is not that you were strong enough to survive?
What if it is that God was merciful enough to sustain you?
What if the story you have been ashamed to tell becomes a testimony to the grace that met you there?
Not because the suffering was good.
Not because the betrayal was justified.
Not because the abuse, injustice, or loss should be romanticized.
But because evil does not have the authority to define the whole meaning of a life surrendered to God.
And here is where Miriam's story becomes even more personal.
Because the woman holding that tambourine was not a flawless woman.
The Bible does not allow us to turn her into one.
Years after the crossing of the sea, Numbers 12 records Miriam and Aaron speaking against Moses.
The account involves criticism concerning Moses' Cushite wife and a challenge to his distinctive prophetic authority.
They asked:
“Hath the LORD indeed spoken only by Moses? hath he not spoken also by us?” — Numbers 12:2 (KJV)
Then Scripture adds a sentence that should make every heart tremble.
“And the LORD heard it.”
The same God who heard Israel's cries in Egypt also heard the words spoken against Moses.
God confronted Miriam and Aaron.
Miriam was struck with a severe skin condition, described in the biblical text as leprous, and she was excluded from the camp for seven days.
Moses cried out to God:
“Heal her now, O God, I beseech thee.” — Numbers 12:13 (KJV)
And the people did not move on until Miriam was brought back.
Do you see the uncomfortable beauty of the biblical account?
Miriam was genuinely used by God.
And Miriam genuinely sinned.
Her earlier faithfulness did not make her incapable of pride.
Her prophetic calling did not place her above correction.
Her worship beside the sea did not mean that every later word from her mouth would honor the LORD.
That should humble every one of us.
Especially those who lead.
Especially those who teach Scripture.
Especially those who sing loudly in church while privately struggling with jealousy, resentment, or the desire to be recognized.
It is possible to celebrate God's power publicly while needing His correction personally.
And it is possible to have a meaningful history of serving God while still needing to repent today.
Miriam's discipline was serious.
But it was not the final scene Scripture gives us of her standing outside the camp.
She was eventually received back.
We must be careful here: Numbers 12 does not provide a detailed account of Miriam's private repentance or describe all that she experienced during those seven days.
But it does show divine correction, Moses' intercession, and her restoration to the community.
And that is enough to confront the lie that correction from God must mean that He has no further concern for us.
Hebrews 12:6 tells us:
“For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth.” (KJV)
God's discipline is not permission for human cruelty, and not every hardship should be interpreted as punishment for a particular sin.
But when Scripture exposes our sin, the faithful response is not denial.
It is humility.
Confession.
Repentance.
And a return to the mercy of God.
Some of you know exactly what that feels like.
You remember seasons when you worshiped with a sincere heart.
When you loved the Word.
When prayer came naturally.
When you wanted nothing more than to please Jesus.
But somewhere along the way, something entered your heart.
Maybe it was bitterness.
Maybe pride.
Maybe compromise that began so quietly you hardly noticed it.
Maybe a hidden habit you promised yourself you would stop.
Maybe jealousy toward someone whose life seemed to be moving forward while yours stood still.
And now you look back at the person you used to be and wonder:
“Was my faith ever real?”
“Have I gone too far?”
“Can God still receive someone who knew better and sinned anyway?”
Listen carefully.
Your sin must not be excused.
But neither should you treat your sin as more powerful than the mercy of Jesus Christ.
The Gospel does not tell you to pretend that you never fell.
It calls you to confess your sin and turn to the Savior who died and rose again.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9 (KJV)
There is no promise here that repentance erases every earthly consequence.
There is something greater.
The promise of forgiveness and cleansing through the faithfulness of God.
And that is why this story cannot end with Miriam.
Because Miriam's tambourine points us to the LORD's victory at the sea, but the full Christian story of redemption brings us to Jesus Christ.
Israel crossed through the sea because God made a way.
We are reconciled to God because Christ made peace through the blood of His cross.
Israel saw the defeat of Pharaoh's pursuing army.
At Calvary, Jesus bore sin and its judgment, and through His resurrection demonstrated His victory over death.
Israel sang on the shore after deliverance.
The redeemed have a reason to praise God because salvation is His gift of grace.
The apostle Paul even connects Israel's passage through the sea with baptismal imagery in 1 Corinthians 10:1–2, while warning believers not to presume upon spiritual privileges without faithfulness.
That warning matters.
The Exodus was never meant to teach that one spectacular spiritual experience makes repentance unnecessary.
And Miriam's life was never meant to teach that an anointed moment excuses an unguarded heart.
Our confidence is not in yesterday's worship.
It is in the living Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (KJV)
Not by the loudness of our songs.
Not by the length of our prayers.
Not by the size of our offerings.
Not by the number of people who admire our ministry.
Not by how convincingly we appear righteous in public.
By grace, through faith.
And that grace does not leave us unchanged.
The next verse, Ephesians 2:10, tells us that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace is not a license to remain in bondage to sin.
It is the gift that brings us into new life with Christ.
This is why the words From Scandal to Grace mean so much.
Not because Jesus promises to erase the historical facts of every scandal.
Not because forgiveness automatically restores broken trust.
Not because redemption guarantees that every earthly relationship, reputation, or opportunity will return.
But because the deepest truth about a repentant sinner need no longer be the sin that once held them captive.
In Christ, there is forgiveness.
In Christ, there is reconciliation with God.
In Christ, there is a new identity.
In Christ, there is power to begin walking in obedience.
Because Jesus rewrites everything that sin once claimed the right to define.
And now I want to speak to the person who has read this far while carrying something nobody around them knows.
The one who smiles in photographs but cries when the room becomes quiet.
The one who knows every worship song but struggles to believe God still loves them.
The parent praying for a child who no longer wants anything to do with church.
The husband or wife trying to rebuild trust after a painful failure.
The young person trapped in shame over choices made in secret.
The believer who has not opened a Bible in weeks because conviction has started to feel unbearable.
You do not need to manufacture a celebration you do not feel.
Miriam sang after a specific act of deliverance, but the Bible also gives us psalms of lament for seasons when tears are the only words we have.
Faith is not measured by whether you can always lift a tambourine.
Sometimes faith sounds like:
“Lord, help my unbelief.”
Sometimes it sounds like:
“Have mercy upon me, O God.”
Sometimes it is the broken prayer of the tax collector in Luke 18:13:
“God be merciful to me a sinner.”
And sometimes the most courageous act of worship is to stop hiding and come honestly before Jesus.
Not with a polished testimony.
Not with religious performance.
Not with promises you intend to keep through your own strength.
But with empty hands and a repentant heart.
Because the Savior who welcomes sinners does not require them to pretend they are already healed.
He calls them to come to Him.
And He is not indifferent to the wounds they carry.
The same Jesus who said, “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden,” also calls His followers to take up their cross and follow Him.
His invitation is both comfort and surrender.
Mercy and truth.
Forgiveness and transformation.
Perhaps your next step is to confess a sin you have concealed.
Perhaps it is to ask forgiveness from someone you have hurt.
Perhaps it is to seek wise pastoral counsel or professional help for a struggle you cannot safely carry alone.
Perhaps it is simply to open the Scriptures again tonight and begin praying.
Whatever obedience looks like in your situation, do not confuse the call to repentance with a demand to earn God's love.
Jesus Christ has already done what you could never accomplish for yourself.
And that changes the way we worship.
We no longer sing to convince God to save us.
We worship because salvation belongs to Him.
We do not give to purchase His favor.
We give because His grace teaches us generosity.
We do not share the Gospel to prove our importance.
We share because the message is too precious to keep to ourselves.
And this is why I believe Miriam's moment beside the sea still matters today.
She did not keep the declaration of God's victory locked inside her own heart.
She called others to sing.
What God had done deserved to be proclaimed.
And in our generation, that same desire to make Christ known can take many forms.
A conversation at the dinner table.
A prayer with a struggling friend.
A Bible shared with someone who has never read it.
A testimony spoken with humility.
Not to impress anyone.
Not to create the appearance of holiness.
But because somewhere among your friends and family may be a person who needs to hear that forgiveness is possible, repentance is necessary, and Christ is mighty to save.
You do not have to reveal private details.
You do not have to tell strangers the things that belong in a safe conversation with someone you trust.
But perhaps you can write:
Or:
“I'm still fighting the good fight of faith.”
Or simply:
“Pray for me.”
And if God has carried you through a season that once seemed impossible, share a little of that testimony if you feel comfortable.
Someone else may be standing at the edge of their own sea, struggling to believe that the Lord has not forgotten them.
Your words may encourage them to seek Him.
Invite your family, your friends, believers who have grown weary, and seekers who are still asking whether the Gospel is true.
We want this community to be a place where the Word of God matters more than appearances, where grace never becomes an excuse for sin, and where broken people are continually pointed to the Savior.
And if you believe in the mission of making faithful Christian teaching and discipleship resources accessible to more people, I want to invite you to consider something deeper.
Not because anyone can purchase a blessing.
But because voluntary, cheerful generosity can be one practical way to participate in work that seeks to glorify Christ.
Scripture teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support for their work (1 Corinthians 9:14), and that God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7).
It is also an invitation to grow alongside a community seeking to become more deeply rooted in Christ.
These free resources remain an important part of our mission.
These are simply resources and expressions of appreciation, never a measure of anyone's spiritual worth.
You can still read, pray, grow, share, and be part of this community.
The Gospel is not for sale.
And the love of Christ cannot be bought.
But if God has given you the desire and ability to help sustain this work, we would be grateful to have you walk with us as a monthly supporter.
Because we must return to that shoreline one final time.
There stands Miriam.
A woman whose life had been marked by oppression.
A sister who once watched a basket among the reeds.
A prophetess who witnessed the power of God.
A worshiper who called the women of Israel to sing.
And, as the rest of Scripture shows, a human being who would still need correction and mercy.
The tambourine did not make her sinless.
Her leadership did not make her the savior.
Her song did not make her the center of the story.
The LORD was the center.
And for us, the fullest revelation of God's saving grace is found in Jesus Christ.
So when you remember Miriam, remember the God who delivered Israel.
When you remember your failures, remember the cross.
When you feel the weight of sin, remember the call to repent and believe the Gospel.
When you are tempted to give up, remember the empty tomb.
And when you finally find the strength to sing again, do not make the song about how extraordinary you are.
Make it about how merciful Jesus has been.
Because one day, every earthly instrument will fall silent.
Every platform will disappear.
Every human achievement will fade.
And the only salvation that can carry us beyond death is the salvation accomplished by Jesus Christ.
Revelation 5:9 portrays the redeemed praising the Lamb who was slain, whose blood purchased people for God from every tribe, language, people, and nation.
That is the greater song toward which the whole story of redemption points.
Not merely the song of people who escaped an earthly enemy.
But the worship of those redeemed by the Lamb.
Miriam's tambourine belonged to a moment in Israel's history.
The glory of Jesus Christ belongs to eternity.
So come to Him while there is time.
Come with your questions.
Come with your grief.
Come confessing your sins.
Come ready to turn from the darkness you have defended for too long.
Come trusting not in your own goodness, but in His death and resurrection.
And if you already belong to Him, keep following.
Keep repenting.
Keep growing.
Keep loving.
Keep telling the truth.
Keep pointing people to Jesus.
Because the goal is not to become a person with an impressive testimony.
The goal is to belong to the Savior whose grace makes any true testimony possible.
And perhaps that is the line I want you to carry with you long after this article disappears from your screen:

The most beautiful thing about Miriam's song was never the tambourine in her hand—it was the God who had brought His people through the waters, and the greater Savior whose grace would one day bring repentant sinners home.
